summary.text: The Younger Dryas was the final climate phase of the Last Glacial Period, lasting from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago.
It is known for abrupt cooling in the Northern Hemisphere, with Greenland chilling by up to 10 °C within a few decades, while the Southern Hemisphere warmed.
The scientific consensus is that a severe weakening of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, or AMOC, explains its climate effects.

facts.label: Local names
facts.value: Nahanagan Stadial in Ireland, Loch Lomond Stadial in Britain

items.prompt: The AMOC ocean circulation strongly affects how much heat crosses the equator. If it weakens sharply, what happens to the two halves of the globe?

options.label: Both hemispheres warm
The North cools while the South warms
Both hemispheres cool equally
The South cools while the North warms

items.explain: With less heat carried north, the Northern Hemisphere cools and the Southern Hemisphere warms: the polar seesaw.

items.prompt: What has historically been the most popular explanation for why the AMOC weakened so badly at the start of the Younger Dryas?

options.label: A flood of fresh, cold lake water into the Atlantic
A sudden drop in the Sun's output
A shift in Earth's orbit
A rapid rise in carbon dioxide

items.explain: The long-favoured idea is an influx of fresh, cold water from North America's Lake Agassiz into the Atlantic.

items.prompt: During the Younger Dryas, most of the Northern Hemisphere cooled. Which season changed the least, or even warmed slightly?

options.label: Winter
Spring
Summer
All seasons cooled equally

items.explain: Winters got much colder and springs cooler, but summers showed no change or even slight warming.

items.prompt: Why is this cold spell named after a small alpine–tundra wildflower?

options.label: The flower was first collected during a cold winter
Its seeds were found inside Greenland ice
It blooms only in the coldest years
Its fossils are common in European sediments of that time

items.explain: Fossils of Dryas octopetala are abundant in European, especially Scandinavian, sediments dating to this period.

items.prompt: Land ice hardly changed during the Younger Dryas, but sea ice spread much farther. Why would that cool the whole planet?

options.label: Sea ice releases cold air as it forms
A bigger icy surface reflected more sunlight
Sea ice blocks volcanic heat from the sea floor
Sea ice soaks up carbon dioxide

items.explain: The extra sea ice raised Earth's albedo, and that increase was the main reason for net global cooling.

items.prompt: Greenland's temperature plunged at the start of the Younger Dryas. How long did that cooling take?

options.label: About 3 years or less
About 300 years
About 3,000 years
About 30,000 years

items.explain: Cooling in Greenland was particularly rapid, taking place over just 3 years or less.

paragraphs.heading: A sudden cold snap
paragraphs.text: The Younger Dryas was the last climate phase of the Last Glacial Period, lasting from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago. It is best known for an abrupt cooling of the Northern Hemisphere. The North Atlantic Ocean cooled, and within a few decades yearly air temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America, 2–6 °C in Europe and up to 10 °C in Greenland. In Greenland the drop took just 3 years or less.

paragraphs.heading: Uneven and seasonal
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile the Southern Hemisphere warmed. The phase ended as fast as it began, with sharp warming over about 50 years that marked the move from the glacial Pleistocene into the present Holocene. The change was not equally quick everywhere: in the tropics the cooling, and the later warming, spread over several centuries. Even in the north, winters got much colder and springs cooler, yet summers stayed the same or even warmed a little.

paragraphs.heading: The polar seesaw
paragraphs.text: In the interval just before, called the Bølling–Allerød, rapid warming in the north was balanced by cooling in the south. This 'polar seesaw' fits with changes in ocean circulation, especially the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, or AMOC, which strongly affects how much heat moves from the Southern Hemisphere to the north. When the AMOC is strong the north warms and the south cools; when it is weak, the reverse happens. Scientists agree that a severe weakening of the AMOC explains the climate of the Younger Dryas.

paragraphs.heading: What weakened the current
paragraphs.text: What made the AMOC so weak is still debated. The long-favoured idea is a rush of cold fresh water into the Atlantic from Lake Agassiz in North America. Meltwater did travel down the Mackenzie River, but sea level did not rise at the time, which may not fit that idea. A newer proposal is a volcanic eruption that started the cooling and sea ice growth, and both ice cores and cave deposits confirm unusually high volcanic activity just before the cold set in.

paragraphs.heading: Named after a flower
paragraphs.text: The period takes its name from Dryas octopetala, a wildflower of alpine tundra whose fossils are plentiful in European, especially Scandinavian, sediments of this age. The flower was also common in two earlier intervals, the Oldest Dryas and the Older Dryas. During the Bølling–Allerød it was rare; instead, Scandinavia was warm enough then to support trees. In Ireland the period is also called the Nahanagan Stadial, and in Great Britain the Loch Lomond Stadial.

paragraphs.heading: Not all at once
paragraphs.text: The cooling was once thought to have begun at about the same moment across the Northern Hemisphere. Varve studies in 2015 instead suggested two stages: first, 12,900–13,100 years ago, around latitudes 56–54°N, and later farther north, 12,600–12,750 years ago. Cores from Lake Suigetsu in Japan and caves in the Philippines show that in East Asia the cold arrived several hundred years later than in the North Atlantic.

paragraphs.heading: Britain in the cold
paragraphs.text: Europe cooled by around 2–6 °C. In the uplands of Great Britain icefields and glaciers formed, while many lowland areas developed permafrost. That implies a mean annual temperature there of no more than −1 °C.
